h1: Warming beers for an Indian winter
title: Warming Beers for an Indian Winter | Craft Beer School
desc: Doppelbock, imperial stout, barleywine, Belgian strong ales and spiced winter beers: what they taste like, how strong they are and how to serve them.
teaser: For a few weeks each year, North India gets cold enough for the beers the rest of the world drinks by the fire.
standfirst: Strong, dark, malty beers make sense when the evenings turn cold. We walk through the main winter styles, what makes them warming and how to serve and share them sensibly.
sections:
Winter means very different things across India. In Delhi, Punjab and Lucknow the nights turn genuinely cold and foggy. In Shimla, Manali or Srinagar it snows. In Bengaluru you might reach for a light jacket after dark. In Mumbai and Chennai you mostly notice that the humidity has eased.

Wherever you are, this is the only stretch of the year when big, strong beers feel natural rather than heavy. Most of the classic warming styles come from places like Bavaria, Belgium, Scotland and England. Their strength, sweetness and fuller body were part of getting through a long cold season.

Warmth in a beer comes mostly from alcohol and malt. Higher alcohol gives a gentle heat in the chest. Rich malt adds caramel, toffee, dark fruit or roast flavours that read as comforting. A fuller body and lower carbonation make the beer something to sip slowly.

All that alcohol has to come from sugar in the wort. Brewers estimate strength with a simple formula: ABV = (OG - FG) x 131.25. A pale lager that starts at 1.048 and finishes at 1.010 lands near 5%. A barleywine that starts at 1.100 and finishes at 1.025 lands near 9.8%. Getting yeast to ferment that far, without stalling or throwing off hot solvent notes, is one of the harder jobs in a brewhouse. It takes a healthy yeast pitch, plenty of oxygen at the start and patient temperature control.
The German lagers: bock and doppelbock

A traditional bock is a strong, malty lager, usually 6.3 to 7.2% ABV, with bready, toasty malt and very little hop character. Doppelbock goes further, typically 7 to 10% ABV, with dark fruit, caramel and a rich, almost chewy body. Many carry names ending in "-ator" in honour of the original monastery beer. Eisbock is concentrated by freezing out some of the water, which pushes the strength higher again. Our guide to bock and doppelbock covers the family in detail.

Imperial stout is the big dark beer most people think of in winter: roasted malt, coffee, dark chocolate and dried fruit at roughly 8 to 12% ABV. Baltic porter is its smoother lager cousin, rich and roasty but cleaner, usually 6.5 to 9.5%.

Barleywine is the strongest of the English tradition, often 8 to 12% ABV, with toffee, caramel and dried fruit. American versions add a lot more hop bitterness. A Scotch wee heavy is malty, caramel-sweet and low in bitterness, with a strength anywhere from about 6.5 to 10%.
Belgian strong ales and spiced winter beers

Belgian brewers make some of the most complex winter beers. A dubbel, around 6 to 7.5%, is dark amber with raisin, plum and caramel. A Belgian dark strong ale, sometimes called a quad, goes to 8 to 12% with fig, date and spice notes. Much of that comes from the yeast itself.

Then there are winter warmers and spiced ales, which use spices like cinnamon, clove and nutmeg. Indian brewers have an obvious advantage here. Jaggery, cardamom, dry ginger and cinnamon from our own kitchens sit beautifully in a dark, malty ale. The trick is restraint. A spice should be a seasoning you notice on the second sip, not a gingerbread latte.

Do not serve these beers ice cold. Strong dark beers show their aromas best around 10 to 13 °C. Straight from the fridge they taste muted and thin. Pour into a tulip glass, a snifter or a wine glass, which holds aroma better than a pint glass.

Pair them with food that matches their weight: slow-cooked mutton, nihari, a cheese board, dark chocolate or a plate of gajar ka halwa, which is a lovely match with a doppelbock.

These beers are strong. A little goes a long way. A 330 ml bottle of a 10% beer holds about as much alcohol as two 330 ml bottles of a 5% lager. Split a bottle between two or three people, pour small measures and drink water alongside. If you are hosting, have good non-alcoholic choices for guests who prefer them. Nobody drives after drinking.

Treated that way, a winter tasting of three or four big beers is one of the best evenings in the beer calendar. It also shows how far style can stretch. Understanding why a doppelbock and a quad end up so different, despite similar strength, is exactly the kind of thing a deeper course on beer styles opens up.
faqs: What beer is best in winter?
Strong, malty, darker styles such as doppelbock, imperial stout, barleywine, Baltic porter or a Belgian dark strong ale. They are sipped slowly and served a little warmer than lager.
At what temperature should I serve strong dark beer?
Around 10 to 13 °C. Colder than that and most of the aroma and flavour stays locked in.
Most fall between 6 and 12% ABV. Check the label and pour smaller measures than you would of a regular lager.
